analysis.one_liner: Required health plans to cover mental illness the same as physical illness and expanded Medicare mental health benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have taxed health plans 25% of premiums unless they covered mental illness like any other illness, never got a hearing or vote and died in committee when Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required employer health plans and insurers to cover treatment for mental illness on the same terms as treatment for physical illness, enforced by a tax equal to 25% of a plan's premiums if it did not. It also would have overhauled Medicare's mental health benefit: replacing the 190-day lifetime limit on psychiatric hospital care with 60 days per year, adding coverage for residential and community-based care and case management, and lowering copays for outpatient mental health and substance abuse treatment.
analysis.who_benefits: People with mental illness or substance use disorders covered by employer or group plans, whose treatment limits, copays, and dollar caps would have to match those applied to physical conditions. Medicare beneficiaries with mental illness or substance abuse would gain new hospital, residential, community-based, and case management coverage, with lower or waived copays for outpatient care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with mental illness and Medicare beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Health plans and insurers could no longer impose limits or cost-sharing on mental health treatment that they did not impose on treatment for other conditions; a plan that failed the standard would owe a tax equal to 25% of its premiums or health coverage expenditures for the year, with exemptions for unintentional failures and mistakes fixed within 30 days.

Medicare's mental health benefit would have been rebuilt: the 190-day lifetime limit on inpatient psychiatric hospital care would be replaced with 60 covered days per year, plus up to 120 days of intensive residential services such as crisis residential programs and residential substance abuse treatment.

Medicare copays for outpatient mental health and substance abuse services would drop, case management would be free and unlimited for seriously mentally ill adults and seriously emotionally disturbed children, and a new category of intensive community-based services (partial hospitalization, psychiatric rehabilitation, in-home services, day treatment) would be covered, with non-physician mental health professionals allowed to supervise treatment plans to the extent state law permits.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers sponsoring group health plans would owe a tax equal to 25% of premiums or plan health expenditures for any year their mental health coverage was less generous than coverage for other conditions, and they would bear the cost of restructuring benefits. The expanded Medicare benefits would be paid by taxpayers through the Medicare trust funds.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, employers with group plans, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The enforcement penalty is unusually steep: a noncompliant plan would owe 25% of its entire year's premiums or health expenditures, a cost that could be passed on to employers and workers through higher premiums rather than absorbed by insurers.

Because 'mental illness' is defined as any condition in the American Psychiatric Association's diagnostic manual, the parity mandate would cover a very wide range of conditions, and the new Medicare coverage of residential and community-based care would significantly increase federal spending.

The bill layered a much stricter standard on top of the narrower parity requirement Congress had already passed in 1996 (which took effect in 1998), and plans would have had to comply for contracts or plan years beginning after December 31, 1998, leaving little transition time for benefit redesign.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The parity mandate is aggressive but mechanically simple: a 25%-of-premiums tax gives insurers and employers a powerful reason to cover mental illness the same way they cover cancer or heart disease, and it includes honest-carve-outs for unintentional failures corrected within 30 days. The real cost question is the price tag — a very large penalty that could show up as higher premiums, a DSM-based definition of covered conditions that is broad, and Medicare expansions that would add substantial federal spending. Set against what it replaced — Medicare's 190-day lifetime psychiatric hospital cap and steep outpatient coinsurance — the benefit to people with mental illness and their families is large, and the bill went far beyond the limited 1996 parity law that Congress actually enacted.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced and to their health subcommittees two weeks later, but neither ever scheduled it for a hearing or vote, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the National Mental Health Parity Act of 1997 on February 5, 1997, joined by Reps. Jim McDermott and Barney Frank as original cosponsors.

The same day, the Speaker referred the bill to both the Ways and Means Committee and the Commerce Committee; it was then sent to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment on February 14 and the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health on February 18.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action was ever recorded; the bill's action history ends with the subcommittee referrals, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

The bill would have gone well beyond the narrower mental health parity provision Congress enacted in 1996 as part of the Health Care Portability and Accountability Act, which the bill's text amends and which took effect for plan years after 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers came out ahead: they never faced the 25%-of-premiums tax or the broad parity mandate, and people with mental illness remained under the much weaker 1996 parity standard and Medicare's 190-day lifetime psychiatric cap.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers avoiding a strict parity mandate

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Democrats or the House's lone Independent and no Republican signed on; because the bill never reached a vote, the record shows only the sponsorship split and the committees, both led by Republicans, that never acted on it.

industries.note: Insurers would owe a tax equal to 25% of premiums any year they limited mental health coverage more than coverage for other conditions, forcing a redesign of benefit and cost-sharing rules. Their interest in keeping restrictive mental health benefits ran directly against people with mental illness.

Self-funded group plans faced the same 25% tax on total health coverage expenditures, so employers would have borne the cost of parity or the penalty. Broader mental health coverage raises plan costs that employers and workers share.

industries.industry: Mental health and substance abuse treatment providers
industries.note: New Medicare coverage of residential, community-based, and case management services, plus parity in private plans, would bring providers more patients able to pay for treatment. The bill also let non-physician mental health professionals supervise care where state law allows.
